page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The mole fraction of a component is the
ratio of the number of moles of that
component to the total number of moles of
all the components in the solution.
steps.why: Concentration can be measured by mass, by volume or by number of particles, and a mole fraction is the third of these. It counts particles against particles, which is exactly what a colligative property responds to, so it is the term Raoult's law and Henry's law are both written in.
common_mistakes: Writing the ratio of masses. A mole fraction counts moles, so each mass has to be divided by its molar mass first.
Dividing by the moles of the solvent alone. The denominator is the TOTAL moles of all the components.
steps.memory_tip: Moles of one component over moles of everything present.
steps.margin_note: The word TOTAL in the denominator is the marked word. Say "all the components", not "the solvent".

steps.label: The equation and the check
lines: For a solution of one solute in one solvent
with n₁ moles of solvent and n₂ of solute:
Mole fraction has no unit and does not
steps.why: Writing both fractions over the same total shows at once why they add to 1, and that sum is the fastest check on any mole fraction calculation. Since only counts of moles appear, nothing in the definition depends on volume, so warming or cooling the solution leaves every mole fraction unchanged.
common_mistakes: Giving the answer a unit such as mol L⁻¹. A mole fraction is moles divided by moles, so it has no unit.
Reporting two mole fractions that do not add to 1. That sum is the check, and it fails when the denominator was wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Every mole fraction is between 0 and 1, and they all add to 1.
steps.margin_note: Write x₁ + x₂ = 1 under the equations. It is one line and it usually completes this mark.
